nameStory: The midsummer tiger swallowtail gets its name from its peak flight period during the height of summer, when most other swallowtails have finished their main emergence. The 'tiger' part comes from the bold yellow and black striped pattern that resembles a tiger's markings, while 'swallowtail' refers to the distinctive tail-like projections on the hindwings.
description: The midsummer tiger swallowtail is a large, striking butterfly with bright yellow wings decorated with bold black stripes and borders. Like other swallowtails, it has characteristic 'tails' extending from the back wings that give the family its name. This species typically has a wingspan of 3-4 inches, making it one of the more noticeable butterflies in New England gardens and woodlands. The females can sometimes appear darker or even blackish, which helps protect them from predators.

idTips.label: Flight timing
idTips.description: Active during peak summer months when other tiger swallowtails are less common, with a distinctive lazy, soaring flight pattern

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Bright yellow wings with bold black tiger stripes running parallel across the forewings, and black borders that feel powdery to the touch if handled

idTips.label: Hindwing tails
idTips.description: Two prominent black-tipped tail projections on each hindwing, along with blue and orange eyespots that shimmer in sunlight

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Large and robust with a wingspan that can cover your palm, with thick, fuzzy body that feels substantial compared to smaller butterflies

idTips.label: Female variation
idTips.description: Females may appear much darker or completely black with reduced yellow markings, but retain the same size and tail structure

idTips.label: Feeding behavior
idTips.description: Often seen nectaring on tall flowers like joe-pye weed and ironweed, with a preference for purple blooms

habitat: Found in deciduous and mixed forests, woodland edges, and suburban areas with mature trees throughout New England. They prefer areas with wild cherry, tulip tree, and ash trees where their caterpillars can develop. You'll often spot adults visiting gardens and parks, especially those with native flowering plants.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not typically active in spring, as this species has its main emergence later in the year.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight period during midsummer (July-August), when adults are most commonly seen nectaring on flowers and engaging in courtship flights. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Late-emerging individuals may still be seen in early fall, though numbers decline significantly. Caterpillars are developing on host trees during this time.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as pupae (chrysalids) attached to host trees, appearing as small brown or green cases that blend with bark.

funFact: This species was only recognized as distinct from other tiger swallowtails in recent decades through DNA analysis - for years, butterfly enthusiasts were seeing them but didn't realize they were looking at a separate species with its own unique midsummer timing!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Eastern Tiger Swallowtail, but the midsummer species flies later in the season when Eastern Tigers are becoming scarce. Remember: if you're seeing fresh, bright tiger swallowtails in the heat of July and August, you're likely looking at midsummer tigers rather than their earlier-flying cousins.
contextualKnowledge: The midsummer tiger swallowtail represents a fascinating example of how modern genetic techniques are revealing 'hidden' species that were long lumped together with their relatives. This discovery reminds us that there's still much to learn about even common, familiar creatures in our own backyards.
compareHints: Compared to the Eastern Tiger Swallowtail, the midsummer species has a distinct later flight period and is often slightly smaller with more vivid coloration. Unlike the Canadian Tiger Swallowtail, which prefers northern regions, the midsummer species is comfortable in warmer, lower elevation areas. The Black Swallowtail lacks the yellow tiger-stripe pattern entirely, making it easy to distinguish.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's swallowtails, Black Swallowtails are the most 'polka-dotted' with their precise yellow spots, while Eastern Tiger Swallowtails are predominantly yellow with black stripes, and Spicebush Swallowtails have greenish-blue highlights with blurry pale markings.
Among New England's swallowtails, spicebush swallowtails are the darkest and most consistently black, lacking the yellow stripes of tiger swallowtails or the yellow spot-bands of black swallowtails.
Among New England's swallowtails, Eastern Tiger Swallowtails are the largest and most boldly striped when yellow.

Unlike the Black Swallowtail which is much smaller and primarily black with blue markings, or the Spicebush Swallowtail which has more blue-green iridescence, the Canadian Tiger Swallowtail maintains its yellow and black tiger pattern in both sexes.
